newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - Lebanon casino a safe bet on stock market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lebanon casino a safe bet on stock market.

text.p: Stunning women in short skirts sipped drinks and cigar smoke drifted over the Casino du Liban's packed roulette tables amid the noise of the slot machines.
But nothing could break Joseph Salami's concentration at 2 a.m. -- not even the fear of losing another $28,000.
He darted from one roulette table to the other, recording each roll of the dice on a small cardboard chart as other customers bought new chips and newcomers filled in membership cards.
So far, the 31-year-old businessman's system of figuring out the odds has failed him. But he and many other gamblers who empty their wallets at the casino keep coming back for more.
Business is booming at the Casino du Liban, former playground of Arab princes and the international jet-set which closed its doors during the 1975-90 civil war and reopened seven months ago.
CASINO RAISES HOPES FOR TOURISM REVENUES

The government sees the casino as a magnet for luring tourists to a country which is pouring billions of dollars into reconstructing war-ravaged Beirut and trying to make jittery foreign investors comfortable.

Company officials hope the reborn casino, perched on a mountainside with a panoramic view over the Bay of Jounieh, will regain its pre-war reputation as a gambling centre that attracted personalities such as King Hussein of Jordan, who enjoyed its famous floor shows.
The casino, meanwhile, is attracting a whole new breed of gambler -- investors armed with calculators as well as stacks of cash.
Beirut stockbrokers say the casino's shares are a hot item on Lebanon's unofficial over-the-counter (OTC) market and they predict long-term market confidence.
The casino's stock was traded at $70 three years ago and is now more than $300 after soaring since it opened its doors and began pulling in big revenues.
"Thirty percent of the OTC market is traded in casino stock," said Michel Aramouni, head of treasury and capital markets at Beirut's Banque Audi.
BROKERS PREDICT HIGH PROFITS
Other brokers are confident of high profits for at least the medium term.

"We have compiled all the figures. We believe the casino's annual turnover could reach as high as $85 million. This would lead to net profits as high as $25 million," said Jean Riachi, chairman of Financial Funds Advisors, a Beirut finance house.
Some brokers believe the Casino's profits could reach $40 million.
Casino shares have risen 93.3 percent on the OTC market this year. They account for $226.8 million of the market's capitalisation of more than $780 million, according to Banque Audi data.
The official Beirut Stock Exchange (BSE), which reopened last year after a 13-year closure in the civil war, trades nine shares of five companies and is capitalised at more than $2 billion.
Both markets are small but offer a window on the business mood in Beirut, once a regional financial and banking centre.
CASINO SPENDS MILLIONS HOPING TO RESTORE GLORY DAYS

The casino has spent $50 million on a facelift to erase the damage caused by the war. A 1,200-seat theatre and two more restaurants will open next year and a five-star, 150-room hotel is to be built beside it by the year 2000.
It is also investing in advertising and its officials make visits to the oil-rich Gulf where they host discreet cocktail parties hoping to entice Arab high rollers armed with petro-dollars.
"We will be making a comeback," said Nicholas Crabtree, of London Club International, which manages the gaming.
"We are pleased with the progress of our casino. The national and international interest is quite staggering." He says 30 percent of the clientele are already Gulf Arabs.
But some market watchers are sceptical.

"The price of the casino's stock is extremely over-valued. I don't think the casino will distribute dividends in the coming few years and the employees will cost too much," said a Beirut broker who did not want to be named.
DIE-HARD GAMBLERS FUEL CASINO'S BALANCE SHEET

But most brokers interviewed by Reuters said the odds were in favour of the casino as it geared up for the busy summer season when gamblers from Saudi Arabia to the small Lebanese towns in the mountains overlooking the bay seek the thrill of the dice.
Just ask a Lebanese millionaire who discussed his strategy after winning $1,500 in one of the casino's exclusive upstairs rooms.
"I drink Lebanese white coffee made of rosewater because it has no caffeine. Caffeine makes me nervous. A good gambler has to stay cool to win," he said.
"I never come here with less than $2,000 in my pocket," he added. "The Lebanese love to gamble."
